title: I'd like tea — sentences where the subject isn't "I"
title_target: मुझे चाय चाहिए — mujhe chaay chaahiye
goal: Order food and say what you need — using a sentence pattern English doesn't have: the person in front isn't "I" but "to me".
bekal: use मुझे, आपको, उसे, and the rest
say what you want with चाहिए
order food and drinks at a restaurant
say you're hungry or thirsty, and how spicy you like it

dialogs.title: संवाद — Lunch at a small eatery
dialogs.intro: Ani has lunch at a small eatery. Look at her first sentence: what stands in front isn't मैं but मुझे. This pattern comes back in units 16 and 17, so get to know it well now.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.literal: question — your — near — vegetarian — food — is?

lines.speaker: वेटर:
lines.id: Yes — dal, vegetables, paneer — we have it all.
lines.literal: ji — yes, dal, vegetable, paneer — all — is.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Then give me dal and two rotis.
lines.literal: so — to-me — dal — and — two — roti — give.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: A bit less spicy. I don't like it too hot.
lines.literal: little — less — spicy. to-me — very — spicy — liking — not — is.

lines.speaker: वेटर:
lines.id: All right. Shall I bring water?

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Yes, and a tea for my friend too.
lines.literal: yes, and — my(fem.) — friend — to — also — one — tea.

lines.speaker: वेटर:
lines.id: If you need anything else, just let me know.

lines.speaker: आनी:
lines.id: Thank you. Bring the bill too, please.

notes: **मुझे is मैं + को — "to me".** Hindi has a group of sentences whose subject stands with को instead of standing bare. *मुझे चाय चाहिए* literally means "**to me** tea is needed", not "I need tea". ⚠️ English has only faint echoes of this ("it seems to me", "it occurs to me"), so don't try to derive it from English. What you can do: learn **the list of verbs**, not the rule. The list is short and it's on the next page.

**चाहिए never changes with the person.** मुझे चाहिए, आपको चाहिए, उसे चाहिए, हमें चाहिए — always the same. That's a relief: one word for everyone. ⚠️ In formal writing चाहिए sometimes becomes **चाहिएँ** when the thing is plural (*मुझे दो किताबें चाहिएँ*), but in everyday speech almost everyone keeps चाहिए.

**चाहिए for things, चाहना for actions.** *मुझे चाय **चाहिए*** = I want tea (the thing). *मैं चाय पीना **चाहती हूँ*** = I want to drink tea (the action). ⚠️ Note that the second sentence goes back to the normal pattern: मैं stands bare, and the verb follows gender as in unit 4. Don't mix them: *मुझे चाय पीना चाहिए* means "I **should** drink tea".

**को also marks the recipient.** *मेरी दोस्त **को** एक चाय* — one tea **for** my friend. With pronouns it shortens: मैं + को → **मुझे**, तुम + को → **तुम्हें**, वह + को → **उसे**, हम + को → **हमें**, वे + को → **उन्हें**. आप + को stays **आपको**.

**तीखा means chili-hot, and the scale may not be the one you know.** Food an Indian calls "a little spicy" often tastes quite hot to visitors — and the heat is of a different kind: more spices, less fresh chili. Lifesaving phrases: **कम मिर्च डालिए** (go easy on the chili) or **बिलकुल तीखा नहीं** (not spicy at all). ⚠️ If it's too hot, drink **दही** or **लस्सी**, not water — water only spreads the burn.

**There's no everyday word for "please".** Hindi politeness lives in the **verb form**: दीजिए, लाइए, बताइए already mean "please give, please bring, please tell". The word **कृपया** does exist but sounds like a station announcement; Indians themselves tend to slip in **ज़रा** (a little) or use the English *please*. Adding **जी** at the end also softens things enough.

**Two table habits worth knowing.** First, eating with your **right hand** is perfectly normal, not bad manners — roti is designed for it. Second, an Indian host will offer more food again and again, and refusing once is taken as mere politeness. If you really are full: **बस, बहुत हो गया, धन्यवाद** — and cover your plate with your palm. ⚠️ For drinking water, ask for a **सील बंद बोतल** (sealed bottle) anywhere you don't know.

grammars.title: Sentences whose subject takes को
body: These sentences cover most of what a beginner wants to say about themselves: want, like, can, hungry, sick. They all use the same pattern.

head: The verb
Example
Meaning
rows: मुझे घर की याद आती है

after: ⚠️ Look at **मुझे हिंदी आती है** — literally "to me Hindi comes". This is how Hindi says "I can speak Hindi", and आती is feminine because **हिंदी** is feminine, not because of the speaker. Compare *मुझे काम आता है* (काम is masculine). Don't confuse this with the rule from unit 4.

grammars.title: Food and drink
after: Tastes: **तीखा** (spicy), **मीठा** (sweet), **नमकीन** (salty), **खट्टा** (sour), **कड़वा** (bitter), **गरम** (hot), **ठंडा** (cold). All end in -आ except नमकीन and गरम, so they change form to match the noun: *मीठ**ी** चाय*, *गरम खाना*.

blocks.text: In Hindi, almost all bodily feelings "happen to" a person rather than being owned by them. So these sentences use को, and the verb follows the gender of the **feeling**, not the person.

blocks.title: Ten sentences that get you through a whole lunch
items: **मेन्यू दीजिए।** — Could I have the menu?
**यहाँ क्या अच्छा मिलता है?** — What's good here?
**यह क्या है?** — What's this? (pointing at the next table's plate — the most successful way to order in India)
**मुझे यही चाहिए।** — I'll have that one too.
**थोड़ा और पानी।** — A little more water.
**बस, बहुत हो गया।** — That's it, that's plenty.
**खाना बहुत अच्छा था।** — The food was delicious.

blocks.text: ⚠️ One cultural difference that often confuses newcomers. In India, **tea comes already mixed with milk and sugar**; if you want it without milk, order **काली चाय** (black tea), and without sugar, **बिना चीनी**. Asking for milk "on the side" as in the West usually earns a puzzled look. On the other hand, **चाय is offered to you everywhere** — in shops, offices, people's homes — and accepting it is the fastest way to start a conversation. Saying no is fine, but accept at least once.

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right को form.
Put the words in the right order.

answers: चाहिए — चाहती हूँ — चाहिए — चाहती हूँ
मुझे एक चाय चाहिए। — मुझे भूख लगी है। — मुझे दो रोटी दीजिए। — मुझे तीखा पसंद नहीं है। — मुझे थोड़ी हिंदी आती है।
मुझे एक चाय चाहिए। — क्या शाकाहारी खाना है? — मुझे तीखा पसंद नहीं है। — मुझे बहुत भूख लगी है। — बिल दीजिए। — बस, बहुत हो गया, शुक्रिया।
